newsitem.title: UKRAINE: ATHLETICS-UKRAINE SAY BAGACH TOOK DRUGS BY ACCIDENT.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-UKRAINE SAY BAGACH TOOK DRUGS BY ACCIDENT.

text.p: Aleksandr Bagach, stripped of his shot gold medal at the world championships in Athens last week for taking a banned substance, faces only "soft sanctions" at home in Ukraine, a sports official said on Wednesday.
Valery Borzov, president of the National Olympic Committee, said Bagach took a natural stimulant containing what Borzov described as "suspect" Chinese herbs.
Bagach had unintentionally taken a banned substance and would therefore receive only an official warning, Borzov said.
"A minimum two-year disqualification can be applied for using serious, hard drugs and stimulants," Borzov said. "In this case they were soft drugs and Bagach took them unknowingly."
Bagach said on Tuesday he was an innocent victim of circumstances.
"It said in the instructions it was a natural product," he said. "One thing is written on the labels and, in fact, it has a different effect."
Borzov, Olympic 100 metres champion in 1972, said tests had become very sensitive and even taking medicine for a common cold could lead to a positive result.
He speculated that hot weather in the Greek capital could have caused the positive test which cost Bagach a gold medal and $60,000 after his 21.47-metre throw was annulled.

"I competed twice with the same stimulant last winter and tested negative," said Bagach, who was banned for two years in 1989 after he was found to have excessive levels of the male hormone testosterone in his body when he was competing for the former Soviet Union.

"After the Athens test I didn't eat for two days and lost a lot of weight. It was too depressing and emotionally tough for me. But I think I won fairly because the drug was very light and, in fact, did not influence the result," he said.
Borzov said he was suspicious about one component of the dru is prepared from a Chinese grass.
He told a news conference on Tuesday that Ukraine needed $2 million to buy a drug-testing laboratory.

"There are no such funds in the state budget. If there were a laboratory there would be no such cases like the one with Bagach," he said. "Without the laboratory, such cases have happened, are happening and will happen."
